newsitem.title: USA: British nanny's lie detector test comes under fire.
newsitem.headline: British nanny's lie detector test comes under fire.

text.p: Prosecutors in the case of a British nanny accused of killing her 9-month-old charge on Monday tried to cast doubts on the validity of lie-detector tests, specifically the one she passed.

Louise Woodward, 19, of Chester, England, is accused of killing Matthew Eappen in February. The infant died as a result of severe head injuries and police have testified that the teenager who came to the United States last summer to work as an au pair violently shook the baby and dropped him on the bathroom floor.
Middlesex Superior Court Judge Hiller Zobel asked forensic psychologist Dr. David Raskin why he did not use the word "drop" when questioning Woodward during her polygraph test.

"She had concerns ... when she was drying the child on the bathroom floor that his head may have bumped against the floor. May have dropped an inch or so -- the thickness of a person's hand," Raskin explained.

Zobel and prosecutor Lincoln Jalelian, during close cross-examination of Raskin -- who was reportedly being paid $3,000 a day for his work -- appeared to doubt the method and accuracy of Woodward's answers, specifically to the question "On February 4, did you deliberately strike or hit Matthew in the head?"

The judge said what troubled him was that the "questions were very narrow and very specific. They leave room for one to think ... (she had) a fair opportunity to answer the questions accurately." But they did not address whether she dropped the infant.
Most of the morning's testimony concerned the accuracy of polygraph tests and the results.

The hearing on whether to allow the polygraph test as evidence in her trial will continue on Monday afternoon. Woodward's trial was scheduled to begin on August 11. She has been jailed since her arrest.
